description: We’re a bunch of curious minds who like asking “what if?” and then actually building the answer We love space, technology, crazy ideas, and turning NASA data into things people can explore, play with, and remember. We’re here to experiment, break things, fix them, probably break them again, and hopefully create something that makes people say, “Wait… you actually built that?
summary: Welcome to Mars Mission: The Lost Signal! For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we didn’t just build a game, we created a Mars survival adventure powered by real NASA data. Meet three astronauts whose mission takes an unexpected turn when an emergency puts their journey home at risk. Now, they must explore the Red Planet, solve problems, and find a way to bring the crew home. They investigate Martian terrain, study geological formations, and search for resources, guided by NASA data. But this isn’t just a story, it’s you in action. As the player, you step into the astronauts’ mission and take on three challenges that turn space science into play, by completing them, you learn how scientists explore Mars, how NASA data reveals its environment, and how decisions can make future missions possible. This is Mars exploration in a new way, not in charts or reports, but through an adventure where every discovery matters, every decision counts, and the crew’s journey home depends on you.
details:
Mars Mission is an educational adventure game designed to teach kids how real space missions deal with danger and limited supplies, turning real NASA data into an interactive story-driven game. Players take care of three stranded astronauts, meet problems on Mars, and use hands-on mini games to solve them, making space science both fun and easy to understand.

The game is a large map of mars , it has several locations and every location has tasks and things to explore , science to understand and decision to make!

In the game, three astronauts, Hedeya, Samantha and Hazaloom, every one of them have the same love for their planet and the same passion to return home to their beolved ones , they land at Jezero Crater on Mars. Then something breaks in their ship , the radio goes silent, and Earth does not know they are stranded. Each astronaut has someone waiting for them back home, someone that loves them deeply , so every choice the player makes is really a choice about getting them home safely. The player is the commander he guide the crew through three missions, in the game he is responsible of bringing them back home safe , and every mission teaches a different part of life on Mars.

Before the adventure starts, the player picks a lead partner. Each partner has a strength and a cost:

  • Hedeya: Stronger shielding and faster air refills at base, but heavier battery gear.
  • Samantha: Saves 15% rover battery and earns bonus science, but has lighter ray protection.
  • Hazaloom: Drives the rover faster and handles rock bumps better, but uses a little more air when walking.

There is no "best" partner, only different ways to play.

Along the way, players keep an eye on three bars: Suit Air, Battery and Shielding. Every choice helps one bar and costs another, just like real mission planners. After each mission, a summary shows what the player gained, what it cost, and the real science behind the choice.

mission 1, The Lost Signal (Communication & Dust Storms): After landing, a blast breaks the return ship and the radio. Players check the damaged spacecraft, grab a spare part, drive the rover to the radio tower and repair it, then rush back to the base before a dust storm arrives. Through this, players learn why spare parts matter, how dust storms affect Mars, and why a message from Mars takes minutes to reach Earth.

Mission 2, The Lava Cave (Radar & Radiation): The crew follows the signal of RIMFAX, NASA's radar that can see underground, into Neretva Vallis, an ancient river valley. Players drop sensors, climb down into a lava tube, drill Rock Core Tube #14 and escape before a Marsquake. A short quiz checks what they learned. Through this, players discover how radar finds hidden layers under the ground and why lava tubes protect astronauts from most space rays.

Mission 3, Rocket Home (Power & Spaceflight): Mars dust jams a rover heater, and it wastes almost all of the rover's 400 W of power. Players first learn what a watt is, then fix the problem on the Power Bus Console: Step 1: Turn off the broken heater. Step 2: Use the extra power for one helper tool (Ray & Dust Shield, Rock Scanner or Battery Boost), and see what each one costs. After that, players drive to the rocket, load the sample, launch, drop the rocket stage at the right moment and dock with the ship that takes them back to Earth. Through this, players learn how to share limited power, and how rockets and docking work.

When the player completes all three missions, the whole crew makes it home!

To keep the game fun to replay, three Mars weather days (Sol 142 Clear, Sol 288 Dusty Sky and Sol 419 Solar Storm) change the radiation, dust and power. Losing is never the end, it is a chance to try a different plan.

The game is made for ages 7 to 12 and runs in the browser, with no account or download. Players can pick an easier Junior level or a Senior level with exact NASA numbers, use Word Helpers for hard words, turn on read-aloud audio, and open the NASA Field Guide to unlock fact cards. Every fact card shows its source and whether the data is live or saved offline. The game uses real data from NASA DONKI, OSDR, Curiosity RAD, Perseverance MEDA, the Deep Space Network, Veggie, RIMFAX and Mars Trek.

The game helps kids, students, teachers and the wider community by:

  • Educating players on radiation, air, power and radio delay through play.
  • Showing how planning and trade-offs keep astronauts safe.
  • Bridging the gap between NASA's datasets and real space missions in a fun, engaging way.

To make NASA's open data more accessible, helping young learners get ready for the challenges of exploring Mars while growing their curiosity about space. Despite our attempt to show how space missions work, our game is simplified for learning, so its numbers and crew abilities are not an exact copy of a real Mars mission. The Mission 1 and Mission 2 cutscenes were made with AI video tools and are only story illustrations.

Coding languages: TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML and CSS.

Frameworks and libraries:

  • React 19 for the menus, crew screens, HUD and mini-game windows.
  • Phaser for the 2D game world: the Mars surface, rover driving, physics and the three missions.
  • Tailwind CSS for styling.
  • Vite to build and run the game.
  • Node.js and Express for a small server that fetches NASA data and falls back to saved data when NASA can’t be reached.
  • Web Audio API for the sound effects, which are generated by code.
  • Lucide icons and Motion for icons and animations.

NASA tools and data: the NASA DONKI API (with a free NASA API key), plus curated data from NASA OSDR, Curiosity RAD, Perseverance MEDA, the Deep Space Network, Veggie and RIMFAX.
